en: And began to address Akjoltoy:
“Akjoltoy, who came between us,
Wisdom’s husbandman, equal to a vast host,
Are you our elder Akjoltoy?
You are our guiding saint who lends us aid,
Our deeply rooted, immovable plane tree,
A thoroughbred who would not weary
Though journeying for six months,
A kinsman who would never abandon us
Whenever hardship came.
Your words are sweet as sugar,
And your gaze is like a lion’s.
Wise master of understanding,
Akjoltoy sees from afar
The calamities of both kin and foe.
Seeking the broad land of Talas,
Seeking the noble hero Kenen,
We came to pitch our camp,
To raise the war cry against
The Chinese khagan in the uplands,
And become true allies.
We exhausted all our horses,
Consumed all our provisions,
And traveled onward in desperate haste,
Galling every mount,
Weighing heavily upon every heart,
Wearing out our colts until they aged,
Exhausting every horse,
Crossing passes and treading over stones,
And pressing mightily onward.
The forty tribes stirred like stars,
Becoming friends until Judgment Day;
We made firm our word of unity
And swore never to part,
And journeyed here of our own will
To settle upon his pastures.
Our wish to become Kenen’s companions
Had long been spoken;
Our two eyes had become four with watching.
We intended to stir battle against the foe,
To keep the heirs of the treasured people
From humiliation by the cruel,
And willingly receive and protect them—
That alone was our purpose.
If we camped beside Kenen,
Smashed the vaunting enemy
And spilled his blood,
And if hardship came to Kangkay,
Stood beside him as support—
That alone was my desire!”
What else could their elder Akjoltoy do?
After the heroes had spoken thus,
Ebegey and Kögöy, the two lions,
Having accepted his skillful counsel,
Resolved wisely and made a covenant,
Binding their promise firmly.
They slaughtered a mare,
And, to become unquestioned kinsmen,
Dipped their hands in its blood.
Reaching agreement in grave words,
Splitting even a black hair exactly in two,
Winning riches wherever they fought,
They became trusted kinsmen.
While matters stood thus,
With a swift and splendid horse
And a letter small as a palm,
Brandishing a tasselled spear,
Zhelzhetpes equipped a messenger
And sent him to hero Kenen,
Entrusting him with the news.
“All that was needed has been set underway;
Baabedin Kenen, baabedin!
Your warriors have joined the host;
Ebegey and Kögöy, the two lions,
Have become your companions!
Led here by God and destined to share your salt,
To settle in the upper reaches of Talas
And become your companions,
The heroes Ebegey and Kögöy have come;
The greatest fortune, prosperity, and happiness
Have come to be yours!”
So the messenger spoke,
Delivering the news.
When he heard these tidings,
The formidable dark-maned lion, the precious warrior,
The precious hero and protector of the people,
Prepared hereditary gifts
For the lions Ebegey and Kögöy,
And went to behold the heroes’ faces.
He chose warriors from among the finest,
Prepared horses from among the finest steeds,
Prepared richly ornamented robes,
And made everything complete and even,
Amassing abundant wealth.
He had the sealed mouth opened
Of the treasury inherited from his fathers,
And its countless worldly riches
Scattered without counting them worth a hair.
There were great herds of all four kinds,
And strong double-humped camels;
When Ebegey and Kögöy arrived,
Every manner of delight was there.
In the hollow of Jylgynduu,
Along the storied Talas River,
Now behold a wondrous sight:
The feast for Ebegey and Kögöy.
The horses’ tails were knotted for competition,
And the splendid games and festivities
Were proclaimed to all the people.
The heroes competed for the goat,
In games that proved a man,
Their splendor surpassing all the people.
Their weight and worth were known among thousands,
Their fierce heroic nature was revealed.
They maintained a royal court and became great lords;
Ebegey and Kögöy, the two lions,
Became khans seated upon golden thrones.
The matchless hero Kenen,
And Akjoltoy, husbandman of wisdom,
Became men of sacred grace.
His support reaching multitudes of people,
They called Kenen the lion of lions,
Saying his valor, fortune, and prosperity
Showed him to be the true lion’s offspring,
A hero who had indeed been found.
The valiant hero Kenen arose,
His fortunes full and equal,
With an iron core and copper arms,
A steadfast dark-maned lion,
A hero and protector of the people.
Ebegey, Kögöy, and Akjoltoy
Acted as those who came between,
And they settled there in peace.
They had stirred the stars in the heavens:
My forefather, the lion Manas,
And Kökbörü of Urum Khan
Had sworn friendship three times in one day.
As a pledge to the hero,
They hunted and ate a wild ass;
“If any offspring remain after me,
Then, in time, the great-hearted lion’s descendant
Shall take Aykanysh,
My daughter,” he had said.
He had made it known to Uskaluu,
Declared it to the caravaner,
And sent a letter by a traveler.
Such was the heroes’ covenant;
If they failed to honor their promise,
They knew it would be shameful folly.
Akjoltoy, husbandman of wisdom,
With Ebegey and Kögöy—the three of them—
Wore out horses and surveyed the land,
Patrolling with spears brandished,
Wearing their horses’ flanks raw,
And ranging across the whole world.
The valiant men of Uskaluu stirred
And came upon the people of Urum.
She was the tempered edge of blue steel,
The cub of Kökbörü,
A scion of the broad valley,
The offspring of the departed hero;
Aykanysh, fiercer than any maiden,
Had bound up her hair like meadow grass
And donned the garb of a saint.
She slept not by day,
And found no rest when night fell.
She now shook out and donned
The twelve arrow-proof layers from the palace;
Each day she tethered and rode
Telkyzyl, whom no arrow could catch.
She made all her weapons ready,
And once more fastened at her waist
The black steel that spilled blood.
She took up the life-taking iron-headed mace
And prepared every piece of equipment.
She gathered many wolf-like champions,
And noble heroes worthy of her,
Appointing Bolot of Urum as commander,
A thickset man of short stature,
Whose whole body was like black stone.
Such was the hero Bolot of Urum;
Aykanysh was a devastating maiden.
Orphaned of her father,
She watched over the land and governed the people,
And was called the accomplished unfortunate one,
Receiving blessings wherever she went.
At Kara-Kyr of Er-Baspas,
Here lay open grazing land,
Where feather grass twisted above the ridge
And wormwood swayed upon the hills,
Where foxtail and white sedge grew—
These were the names of its grasses.
From the warm slopes curled
Black meadow grass and brocade-like flowers,
And grasses of every kind swayed.
She rode out into the open country.
It was a land of rolling hills and hollows,
Where springs flowed in torrents,
And nightingales sang sweetly,
Where eagle-owls hooted and called,
And nightingales displayed themselves in the willows,
Where cuckoos called from the birches
And roe deer cried in the thickets;
It was a land beyond compare,
Kara-Kyr of Jan-Baspas,
Known as the Kara-Kyr uplands.
When she came to that place,
Two men approached, riding tawny thoroughbreds
And carrying broad, long spears.
Like storm clouds returning with rain,
Wrath circled across their faces.
Their eyes were like opened grain pits,
Their faces like grains of oiled wheat;
They were tall and broad-shouldered,
Their massive bones like a fortress,
As though those who fought them would be crushed to flour.
Their ears were like shields,
Their bright eyes like the morning star.
Throwing the whole world into alarm,
They made the thoroughbreds beneath them
Pace forward with stately strides.
Blood burned from their fury,
And life itself sprang from their courage.
Tall as plane trees and rich in wisdom,
They were strikingly handsome, with imposing faces
And broad front teeth like gates.
Their deeds surpassed all others in the world.
They had a splendid red camel,
And loaded upon that camel
Was every treasure of this fleeting world.
Their majesty was great and their wrath was fierce;
Mighty husbandmen of wisdom,
Two men appeared before her.
They wore armor no arrow could pierce;
Ebegey and Kögöy rode at their head,
And behind them came a thousand troops.
When that army moved, it rumbled like an earthquake;
If one of its leaders unleashed destruction,
He could devour six thousand men.
With short stirrups and broad shoulders,
They bore formidable spears and battle-axes,
Their weapons and gear fully prepared.
Joybolot, the unsheathed sword,
Would not leave their side even in death.
When they met and raced one another,
Their paired swift steeds, beyond an arrow’s reach,
Seemed to grapple with their mouths;
Akjoltoy and the hero Seytek were coming.
Their appearance and majestic bearing
Could reach a man’s soul without tiring,
And their courage could make the black earth
Quake and tremble beneath them.
Bolot opened his eyes and saw them;
Seeing them, Bolot was astonished.
The reins went slack and were drawn tight,
